name: Marius Mercator
knownFor: A Latin writer, a correspondent of Augustine of Hippo, who warned the church of Constantinople against the followers of Pelagius and put the sermons of Nestorius into Latin.
dates: Gave his Commonitorium on Caelestius to the church of Constantinople in 429, by the consuls its title names. No ancient source used here gives his birth or death. Garnier, his first editor, thought he wrote nothing after the Council of Chalcedon; Baluze thought he lived past it
role: Translator and writer against the Pelagians and Nestorius

keyWorks.title: Commonitorium on Caelestius
keyWorks.about: a warning written in Greek in 429 to the church of Constantinople and offered to the emperor Theodosius the Younger; he put it into Latin himself

keyWorks.title: Latin translations of Nestorius
keyWorks.about: sermons and letters of Nestorius, with letters of Cyril of Alexandria, turned into Latin for Western readers

keyWorks.title: Book of Notes against the Words of Julian
keyWorks.about: answers to Julian of Eclanum, tracing the error back to Theodore of Mopsuestia

traces: Hefele, the historian of the councils, says the twelve anathemas Nestorius set against Cyril of Alexandria survive only in his Latin.
His volume carries much of the Nestorian and Pelagian record to Latin readers, in his own translations.
remembered: Augustine of Hippo writes to him as "my son" and says he had not known how far Mercator had come.
Garnier notes that even Gennadius of Marseilles does not name him.

uncertain: Little is known of his life, and no ancient writer tells it. Garnier, his first editor, notes that even Gennadius of Marseilles leaves him out.

His origin is disputed. Garnier guessed southern Italy, from his knowledge of Caelestius and Julian of Eclanum. Baluze guessed Africa. Schoenemann says both views are conjectures. B. B. Warfield, in his introduction to Augustine's anti-Pelagian writings, calls him an African layman.

That he was a layman is an inference. Garnier draws it from Augustine calling him son and not brother, and from his absence among the bishops at Ephesus. Hefele calls him a layman living in Constantinople. Garnier says copyists wrote "bishop" for "letter" in Possidius's list of Augustine's works.
The year of Augustine's letter to him is Garnier's reckoning (418). Augustine's letter is held only in Latin.
He wrote as a partisan against Nestorius, Julian and Caelestius. The rumours about Caelestius and Julian that Garnier gathers from him are an opponent's.
When he died is unknown. Garnier thought he wrote nothing after the Council of Chalcedon; Baluze thought he did, since he names the followers of Eutyches.
